content: Articles are intended to provide useful information to readers. This information can include the latest news, knowledge about a particular topic, guides, or analyses.
title: Articles

content:
TL;DR Evaluation design: 90 test cases, a read-only database sandbox, single-turn interaction, 3 generative models × 3 systems (direct → direct+rag → harness), each run once. Retrieval is the only order-of-magnitude gain: adding retrieval alone lifts EX from 6.9%~32.9% to 43.8%~54.8%, and lifts the behavior decision from the zero-ability line to 79%~90% balanced accuracy. The output contract layer only buys a layer of post-processing: its EX gain shrinks as the baseline’s own executability rises (Qwen +11.0 → V3 +2.8 → flash 0.0, and only the Qwen point sits outside the jitter band). What it really fixes is output hygiene. In single-turn interaction, the Agent architecture’s value is carried mainly by retrieval and the prompt. Retrieval is, in essence, data processing over text, and text is data too, so in the single-turn setting this Agent’s value comes almost entirely from text data engineering. Scope: it covers single-turn SQL generation only, and leaves out multi-turn, exploration routing, execution and result analysis. Abstention behavior is the most model-sensitive: flash never abstains and its behavior collapses back to the zero-ability line, while Qwen is good at clarify and V3 at refuse. The main differences likely come from post-training and decoding rather than architecture. 1. Background and Goal # The NL2SQL Agent translates natural-language questions into SQL queries. Its core design is to ask a clarifying question first when information is insufficient, mimicking real human interaction, rather than forcing an answer. The project started in March 2025, and a detailed write-up is in the portfolio: NL2SQL Agent: Ask Before You Query.
Over the past year, the harness idea has grown more popular and models have kept getting stronger, which raised a question for me: does the NL2SQL Agent I built back then actually have an ask-first advantage? That question is what produced this evaluation design and evaluation.
xifanz42/nl2sql_agent 轻量化自然语言数据库查询工具，支持多轮对话完善查询目标，精确输出SQL查询语句、执行查询、数据分析并返回自然语言结果。A lightweight system enbales multiple rounds of chat to transfer natural language into SQL query, execute query, perform data analysis and return analysis results. Python 16 2 2. Evaluation System Design # At first I used a golden-standard dataset of 90 cases and simply compared the NL2SQL Agent against a direct LLM call. The result was that the evaluation design was too crude, and it could not evaluate the act of asking a clarifying question at all. The main problems:
The dataset was not rigorous enough: 13 cases referenced metrics that do not exist in the database, so every system would necessarily score 0 on them; 27 cases treated text columns as dates, even though in the database those date values are stored as text (this was deliberate, originally meant to test the NL2SQL Agent’s ability). The test-case design contradicted the test goal: the dataset had only a question column and an expected-SQL column, so every case implicitly required SQL output. That scoring rule turned into rewarding guessed SQL and punishing clarifying questions, which is the exact opposite of the system’s design goal. The metric design was too narrow: metrics focused on SQL-generation accuracy and schema consistency, which, just like the problems above, also punished clarifying behavior. A system that correctly asks the user a question would instead be marked as producing a wrong output. So after several iterations, the later evaluation experiments follow two principles:
Every test case must state its expected behavior explicitly: answer directly with SQL, ask for clarification, or refuse to answer? Metrics must not be aggregated into a single number, but evaluated along several dimensions. The four sections below all describe the improved evaluation system design (dataset adjustments, test-case design, systems under test, metric design, and so on).
2.1 Dataset # The evaluation data is a simulated vehicle-KPI table kpi_benchmark for a port-logistics site, stored in PostgreSQL:
Category Content Scale 360 rows spanning 6 days (2025-08-15 ~ 08-20), all recorded at 00:00:00Z Dimensions vehicle_id, vehicle_type (AT automated transfer vehicle / MT manual vehicle) Metrics 3 index_category values, 10 concrete metrics index_name, metric values index_value 2.2 Test Case Design # 2.2.1 Expected-Behavior Categories # Building on the analysis above, the 90 test cases were split into 3 expected behaviors: answering the SQL query (answer), asking for clarification (clarify), and refusing to answer (refuse). The final split is 73 answer, 3 clarify, 14 refuse.
Situation N Expected behavior Explanation The user asks about a metric that does not exist in the database 13 refuse No executable query exists, so any answer would be fabricated Depends on CURRENT_DATE, so results drift with the date 1 refuse No stable, reproducible correct answer The question is vague, with several queryable directions 3 clarify The user needs to supply the metric or range The rest 73 answer The question is clear and the data is sufficient 2.2.2 Difficulty Strata # Besides the behavior categories, the cases were also split into difficulty strata by the syntactic features of the SQL. Here hard concentrates on multi-condition filtering, subqueries and time aggregation, and this classification measures the complexity of the query itself.
Stratum Rule (any one qualifies) N easy Single-table equality filter only 3 medium Contains GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIMIT, BETWEEN, LIKE, DISTINCT, IN, or multi-condition AND / OR 46 hard Contains JOIN, subqueries (multiple SELECT), window functions (OVER, WITHIN GROUP, FILTER), HAVING, EXTRACT, INTERVAL, CASE WHEN, UNION, STDDEV, CURRENT_DATE 24 2.3 Systems Under Test # Three systems take part in the evaluation, all driven by the same prompt template:
System Role Prompt Retrieval Output contract layer direct Bare-LLM baseline same as harness no no direct+rag Retrieval-augmented baseline same as harness yes no harness The NL2SQL Agent project, the main target same as harness yes yes All three share the same system prompt, the same schema injection, the same retrieval implementation, and the same generative model with the same decoding parameters. Each case makes exactly one model call. So only two independent variables remain between them:
Whether there is retrieval (direct vs direct+rag) Whether there is an output contract layer (direct+rag vs harness) 2.3.1 Output Contract Layer # A post-processing chain unique to harness. Its starting point is distrust of the model’s free text: it treats the reply as a string to be parsed and reduces it, with sentinels, regexes and a whitelist, into a binary outlet the evaluation can read (SQL present / SQL absent).
# Component Purpose 1 Three-way sentinel parsing Splits on SQL_QUERY: / 请提供具体信息: / 引导提问: to decide which action the system chose 2 SQL extraction and normalization Must contain SQL_QUERY:; strip markdown fences; cut at the first ;; append ; 3 SQL validation guardrail Dangerous-keyword plus unknown-table check; on failure it returns an error message Note that here a SQL parse failure and a guardrail rejection are both marked as declining to answer in the later trials. That is indistinguishable, in the data, from the model itself declining because of insufficient information or an unreasonable request. This is why the quality axis and the behavior axis share the same outlet, and it is a precondition to keep in mind when attributing results in §3.3.3.
Two changes relative to the product implementation: the follow-up check short-circuits to False when there is no conversation history (in a single-turn evaluation it neither affects the prompt nor produces that helper call); and the generation temperature is changed from the product’s 0.7 to 0.0, to align with the baselines (see §2.3.3).
2.3.2 Model Selection # The same three-system structure is run once on each of three generative models. Their structure and specs:
Label Provider Model name Architecture Activated / total params Notes Qwen-Coder SiliconFlow Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct MoE (128 experts, 8 activated, GQA) 3.3B / 30.5B Code-specialized; 262K context DS-V3 SiliconFlow deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3 MoE (256 routed experts + 1 shared; MLA; MTP) 37B / 671B General-purpose flagship; 128K context DS-Flash DeepSeek API deepseek-flash (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) Causal-Encoder-Decoder MoE (asymmetric input/output) 8B input / 16B output / 552B Lightweight general tier; natively multimodal; non-thinking mode in this article These three models cover three shapes: activation scale (3.3B activated vs 37B activated), domain bias (code-specialized vs general), and cost tier (light vs flagship).
Note that flash’s “lightweight” refers to its activation scale and cost tier, not its total parameters. Its Causal-Encoder-Decoder architecture pushes input-side activation down to 8B and output-side to 16B, and greatly compresses the KV Cache, so both unit price and cache cost are lower. All three accept the same set of decoding parameters (temperature=0, max_tokens=4096), and the DeepSeek endpoint has thinking mode turned off (§2.3.3).
Model spec sources: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-V3 from their public model cards; DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from the official DeepSeek announcement (2026-09-10). 2.3.3 Other Controlled Variables # Variable Value How it is controlled system prompt Identical Shared render_prompt, compared by a test assertion schema injection Identical render_prompt inlines schema_info Retrieval direct none; the other two share one function direct+rag calls the agent’s own retrieve_knowledge Generative model Same model within a run Fixed by --provider/--model, written to the ledger temperature 0.0 call_coder and the baseline request read the same constants, so they cannot drift apart max_tokens 4096 Identical for both, to avoid truncation from a lower cap Thinking mode Off extra_body={"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}} (only the DeepSeek endpoint has this switch) Conversation history Always empty Single-turn evaluation Database Read-only role A least-privilege connection from EVAL_DATABASE_* 2.4 Metric Design # Building on the first round of evaluation, the metric design is now split into 3 groups.
One group is the metrics most common in the NL2SQL literature, used to score the quality of the SQL expression, the quality metrics. Another is the group this evaluation mainly tests, which scores the relationship between the system’s behavior and the expected behavior, the behavior metrics. Besides those, there is a group of cost-related economic metrics covering response latency, tokens and LLM calls, used to judge whether using the NL2SQL Agent is economical.
2.4.1 Quality Metrics # Metric Definition Direction valid_sql SQL syntactic validity (whether it runs) up exact_match (EM) Exact match: the string equals the reference SQL up execution_match (EX) Execution match: after execution, the result set equals the reference result up schema_adherence Data-model consistency: referenced tables and columns all exist in the database schema up EX@answered Conditional execution match: EX computed only on cases the system actually answered up Besides the four conventional quality metrics, this round introduces EX@answered (Conditional EX). The reason is that only 73 of the 90 cases are truly answerable, while the other 17 expect a clarifying question or a refusal. So the EX computed directly over the answerable set (N=73) actually aggregates two independent abilities:
Willingness to answer (coverage) Accuracy when answering (EX@answered) The three quantities EX, EX@answered and Coverage always satisfy:
\[ \mathrm{EX} = \mathrm{Coverage} \times \mathrm{EX@answered} \]Note that \(\mathrm{EX} = \mathrm{EX@answered}\) holds if and only if \(\mathrm{Coverage} = 100\%\).
2.4.2 Behavior Metrics # Because the system’s clarifying questions and, conversely, its refusals to answer would be judged as wrong behavior and penalized by the quality metrics above, a separate set of metrics is needed to score the system’s behavior. My approach here is to borrow from data science and statistics and reduce it to a standard binary classification problem: treat “the system should answer” as the positive class, so each case ends in one of only two behaviors:
Answer (answer, 73 cases) Do not answer (clarify + refuse, 17 cases). That gives a standard 2×2 confusion matrix:
Actual: answered Actual: not answered Expected: answer TP FN Expected: not answer FP TN This is in fact a classic, standard binary-classification problem, so the metrics it yields are the usual statistical ones. This evaluation simply gives them domain names, so the derivations are omitted:
Domain name Standard statistic Formula Denominator (conditional sample space) Direction presumption_rate False positive rate FPR \( \dfrac{FP}{FP+TN} \) 17 (should not answer) down over_clarify_rate False negative rate FNR \( \dfrac{FN}{FN+TP} \) 73 (should answer) down policy_accuracy Accuracy \( \dfrac{TP+TN}{N} \) 90 (all) up balanced_accuracy Balanced Accuracy \( \dfrac{\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR}}{2} \) 90 (all) up Specificity TNR \(= TN/(TN+FP) = 1-\mathrm{FPR}\) is the other side of the same coin as the presumption rate, so below it is recorded uniformly as “not-answer recall” and not listed as a separate metric.
Note that policy_accuracy (Accuracy) can only be a reference, because it folds the dataset’s class mix into the score: Accuracy is a weighted average of \(\mathrm{TPR}\) and \(\mathrm{TNR}\) with the class prior \(\pi = P(\text{should answer})\) as the weight, and \(\pi\) is set by the dataset, not by system ability. This article therefore also introduces balanced_accuracy, which averages the two class recalls with equal weight to remove that weighting. The derivation of this metric and its measured comparison on this data are in §3.3.2.
2.4.3 Cost Metrics # Cost has to answer two different questions, so it is split into two groups: economic cost decides “is this system worth deploying”, and experience cost decides “can the user stand the wait”. All are measured over the 90 cases:
Group Metric Meaning Use Economic calls per case How many LLM requests each case makes on average All three are 1 (the follow-up check short-circuits without conversation history, so it makes no call) Economic tokens per case Total input + output tokens per case Measures context size Economic cached share Share of input tokens that hit the provider’s prompt cache Affects unit price: the cached part is billed at the cache price Economic cost per 1k cases Spend per thousand cases, in CNY (= per-case cost × 1000) Estimated from token counts × a dated price list, see below; this article reports costs in this unit throughout Experience latency p50 / p95 Median / 95th percentile of end-to-end response time The wait the user actually feels Do not conflate the two. In the measurements their drivers are almost orthogonal: tripling the input tokens raises p50 by only 0.05–0.18 s, while switching model or provider tier is a factor of 3.8 (§3.4).
The per-case cost is computed as
\[ \mathrm{Cost} = \frac{(\text{prompt} - \text{cached}) \cdot p_{in} \;+\; \text{cached} \cdot p_{cache} \;+\; \text{completion} \cdot p_{out}}{10^{6}} \]where \(p_{in}, p_{cache}, p_{out}\) are the unit prices for input / cached input / output (CNY per 1M tokens), recorded in app/eval/pricing.py with sources and dates (SiliconFlow 2026-09; DeepSeek official 2026-10).
Price is an external variable. A cost figure holds only for this dated price list; latency and call counts are not part of economic cost.
The DeepSeek API price also fluctuates by time of day (Beijing time, weekdays 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–18:00 are peak; other hours, weekends and holidays are half price). The price list takes the peak price, so the DeepSeek cost figures are an upper bound, not a lower bound.
3. Results # 3.1 Overall Table # The table below is all nine cells (the 3 × 3 model-by-system combinations); the denominator for Coverage is the 73 answerable cases. Cost and latency are not on this axis, they form their own group (§3.4). The per-metric breakdown is in §3.2–§3.4.
Model System EX EX@answered Coverage valid_sql presumption rate down over-clarify rate down policy accuracy balanced accuracy Qwen3-Coder direct 6.9% 20.8% 32.9% 26.0% 17.6% 67.1% 42.2% 57.6% direct+rag 43.8% 48.5% 90.4% 76.7% 11.8% 9.6% 90.0% 89.3% harness 54.8% 59.7% 91.8% 90.4% 11.8% 8.2% 91.1% 90.0% DeepSeek-V3 direct 9.6% 58.3% 16.4% 16.4% 5.9% 83.6% 31.1% 55.3% direct+rag 53.4% 62.9% 84.9% 79.5% 5.9% 15.1% 86.7% 89.5% harness 56.2% 67.2% 83.6% 83.6% 17.6% 16.4% 83.3% 83.0% deepseek-flash direct 32.9% 32.9% 100.0% 97.3% 100.0% 0.0% 81.1% 50.0% direct+rag 54.8% 54.8% 100.0% 89.0% 41.2% 0.0% 92.2% 79.4% harness 54.8% 55.6% 98.6% 87.7% 29.4% 1.4% 93.3% 84.6% The relationship between the three systems forms a chain:
direct ──add retrieval──▶ direct+rag ──add output contract layer──▶ harness 3.1.1 Reading Preconditions # Measured drift from repeated runs of the same configuration:
Model · System EX, first pass EX, second pass Δ EX Δ balanced accuracy Δ policy accuracy Qwen · direct 9.6% 6.9% −2.7 +5.2 +1.1 Qwen · direct+rag 48.0% 43.8% −4.1 +2.3 0.0 V3 · direct 9.6% 11.0% +1.4 −0.2 +3.3 V3 · direct+rag 53.4% 49.3% −4.1 −2.9 −1.1 V3 · harness 56.2% 54.8% −1.4 +1.5 −1.1 With the same configuration, the same prompt and temperature=0, the metrics still drift. The reason is that one component (TNR) has a denominator of only 17, so a single case is 5.9%. This is not a flaw in the experiment; it is the default property of any single-run LLM evaluation: temperature=0 is only “greedy decoding”, and server-side MoE expert routing and continuous batching still introduce jitter.
So differences below roughly 5 percentage points should not be interpreted. This is the reading precondition for every conclusion in this article.
3.1.2 Net Effect of the Contract Layer # From direct+rag to harness, the only architectural variable that is added is the output-contract-layer processing. And the output contract layer leaves a trace in only these three places, all far smaller in magnitude than retrieval:
Model ΔEX Δvalid_sql Δ balanced accuracy Qwen +11.0 (43.8 → 54.8) +13.7 (76.7 → 90.4) +0.7 (89.3 → 90.0) V3 +2.8 (53.4 → 56.2) +4.1 (79.5 → 83.6) −6.5 (89.5 → 83.0) flash 0.0 (54.8 → 54.8) −1.3 (89.0 → 87.7) +5.2 (79.4 → 84.6) From the differences of each metric between direct+rag and harness:
The contract layer’s gain has very few detectable points. Only under the Qwen model does the system change reach a gain of +11.0. This is because the contract layer essentially solves an output-hygiene problem: Qwen goes from 10 broken cases to 1, V3 from 4 to 0, and flash’s 8 cases stay at 8. Whether it can be fixed depends on how hygienic the model’s output is, which is exactly why its EX increment is detectable only under Qwen. On cost, this layer costs nothing at all; it is a purely software-side post-processing step.
3.2 Quality Metrics # 3.2.1 EX # Using the three components from §2.4.1, each EX cell can be decomposed (\(n_A\) is the number of answered cases among the 73 answerable, \(c\) the number of those with a correct result set; it always holds that \(\mathrm{EX} = \mathrm{Coverage} \times \mathrm{EX@answered}\)):
Model · System \(n_A\) \(c\) \(\mathrm{EX}=c/73\) \(\mathrm{EX@answered}=c/n_A\) \(\mathrm{Coverage}=n_A/73\) Qwen · direct 24 5 6.9% 20.8% 32.9% Qwen · direct+rag 66 32 43.8% 48.5% 90.4% Qwen · harness 67 40 54.8% 59.7% 91.8% V3 · direct 12 7 9.6% 58.3% 16.4% V3 · direct+rag 62 39 53.4% 62.9% 84.9% V3 · harness 61 41 56.2% 67.2% 83.6% flash · direct 73 24 32.9% 32.9% 100.0% flash · direct+rag 73 40 54.8% 54.8% 100.0% flash · harness 72 40 54.8% 55.6% 98.6% From the table above:
Retrieval is the largest single gain: with the same model and the same prompt, adding RAG alone raises EX substantially. But the way each model degrades without retrieval is different: Qwen guesses but guesses wrong (answers only 24 cases, EX@answered just 20.8%); V3 answers conservatively (answers only 12 cases, yet EX@answered is 58.3%); flash answers everything with full confidence, blindly (all 73 answerable cases answered, and all 17 unanswerable cases also turned into SQL). 3.2.2 Executability # The denominator of valid_sql is the 73 answerable cases, so it reads as “how many cases produced SQL that runs”. Here, using the same approach as EX@answered, we split out conditional valid SQL: \[P(\text{executable} \mid \text{answered})\]Like EX, valid_sql decomposes into two independent factors:
\[ \mathrm{valid\_sql} = \mathrm{Coverage} \times P(\text{executable} \mid \text{answered}) \] Model · System answered /73 executable /73 valid_sql answered but won’t run executable given answered Qwen · direct 24 19 26.0% 5 79.2% Qwen · direct+rag 66 56 76.7% 10 84.8% Qwen · harness 67 66 90.4% 1 98.5% V3 · direct 12 12 16.4% 0 100.0% V3 · direct+rag 62 58 79.5% 4 93.5% V3 · harness 61 61 83.6% 0 100.0% flash · direct 73 71 97.3% 2 97.3% flash · direct+rag 73 65 89.0% 8 89.0% flash · harness 72 64 87.7% 8 88.9% After this further decomposition of valid_sql, we can answer “among the generated SQL that runs, how good is the SQL?”. The table shows that adding RAG makes the model more willing to answer, but does not improve the quality of the SQL expression. Coverage goes 16.4% → 32.9% → 100.0% up to 84.9% → 90.4% → 100.0%; but V3 and flash’s P(executable | answered) actually regress, and Qwen is the only one that rises. Looking at the run logs, the failures fall into two kinds: SyntaxError, and calls to functions that do not exist in the database (UndefinedFunction). The two are different in nature:
Qwen’s syntax errors are almost all markdown fence leakage. It wraps the SQL in ``` and outputs it, so Postgres reports syntax error at or near "```". This is not wrong SQL, it is an output hygiene problem; harness’s contract layer strips the fences, which is exactly why it fixes those 10 cases down to 1 (§3.1.2). But narrowing the scope to executable SQL, Qwen is still the worst on hard (3/13), so its gap is “output hygiene + genuinely wrong SQL” stacked together. flash’s failures are all missing functions. Once retrieval injects the schema and the metric descriptions, flash starts writing more complex aggregations, but calls functions that do not exist in the database. 3.3 Behavior Metrics # In the dimensions below we only look at whether the system chose answer or abstain on each question, which is unrelated to whether the SQL was accurate. A system can output a correct SQL expression and still be guessing on every answer.
3.3.1 Presumption Rate and Over-Clarify Rate # The left side of the figure is the presumption rate (of the 17 cases that should be declined, how many were answered), and the right side is the over-clarify rate (of the 73 cases that should be answered, how many were questioned). The dashed line represents the “judge nothing” extreme: answer everything gives a presumption rate of 100%, decline everything gives an over-clarify rate of 100%.
Looking at the left side alone, qwen3-coder and v3 both do well (17.6% & 5.9%), meaning they do not rush to output SQL on unclear questions. But the price of their low presumption rate is the highest over-clarify rate in the table (67.1% & 83.6%). By contrast, flash sits at the other extreme: an extremely low over-clarify rate (close to 0 in all three systems), at the price of the highest presumption rate in the table.
From the system’s point of view, adding retrieval clearly helps. Which side it improves depends on which extreme the model was stuck at: Qwen and V3 were stuck at “over-clarify”, so retrieval mainly improves that side (Qwen from 67.1% → 9.6%, V3 from 83.6% → 15.1%); flash’s over-clarify rate was already 0%, so retrieval improves its presumption rate instead (100.0% → 41.2%).
Because the presumption rate and the over-clarify rate are driven by the same “should I answer” threshold, the scatter plot below shows each system under each model more directly:
In this plot the x-axis is the presumption rate and the y-axis the over-clarify rate. The ideal outcome is a system with complete question recognition and correct behavior decisions, i.e. the origin at the bottom left (the ideal point). The worst case is a system with no ability to tell questions apart, which lands on the dashed line in the figure (the zero-ability line). flash direct is the measured sample of exactly that: all 17 unanswerable cases were turned into SQL (presumption rate 100.0%), while not one was questioned (0.0%), so behaviorally it is fully equivalent to “always answer”, a zero-ability classifier. From these 3 scatter plots, retrieval’s (RAG’s) improvement to system ability is more visible: whichever model a system uses, the direct+rag system is closer to the origin.
3.3.2 Balanced Accuracy # Now let us look at the three systems’ output from the angle of policy accuracy. Because the TP and TN samples in these test cases are not balanced, this article also introduces balanced_accuracy, which averages the two class recalls with equal weight. (See §2.4.2 for the behavior metrics.)
A concrete comparison shows why balanced accuracy is the better metric to read. Under the flash model, the direct system’s policy accuracy is 81.1% (exactly the majority-class share, 73/90), while its balanced accuracy is 50.0%. Reading only policy accuracy, one would think the system’s behavior decisions were decent; reading balanced accuracy, one sees that the system’s behavior ability is 0 (see the figure).
The figure is the balanced accuracy after averaging the two class recalls with equal weight; the dashed line is the zero-ability line. Landing on the line means the system’s behavior decisions are no better than random guessing.
The figure shows that all three systems’ direct stops near the zero-ability line, within 8% of each other, and the gap between neighbors is less than a single case on the TNR side (1/17 = 5.9%), so all that can be read here is “none of them has behavior-decision ability”.
After adding retrieval, the three systems’ behavior-decision ability rises to 79.4%, 89.3% and 89.5% respectively, about a 30% improvement over each system’s own direct. The mechanism makes sense: without retrieval, the model cannot tell “whether this metric name exists, whether the question has a unique solution”, so it can only guess; retrieval turns “should I decline” from a guess into something judgeable.
Combining balanced accuracy with the presumption rate and over-clarify rate above, we can see that adding retrieval can substantially raise a system’s behavior-decision level.
3.3.3 Abstention Behavior # In this experiment there are 90 test cases in total, split by expected behavior into three kinds (§2.2.1): 73 that should be answered, 14 that should be refused (refuse, asking about metrics that do not exist in the database) and 3 that should be clarified (clarify, the question itself being ambiguous). What this subsection calls “abstention” refers to the 17 test cases where the system should not output SQL.
The figure shows abstention behavior in detail: the x-axis is the three models, and in each group the three bars from left to right are direct, direct+rag, harness; the left panel is the 14 refuse cases and the right panel the 3 clarify cases; the closer to the dashed line, the more the behavior matches the expectation.
Looking at the detailed output logs, although both expected behaviors are classed as abstention, they are essentially different abilities, provided by two different things:
Ability Missing Provided by In practice refuse Which metrics actually exist in the database Business text in the knowledge base Rises sharply once retrieval is added, and by harness all three are level at 12/14 (flash starts from 0: 0 → 10 → 12) clarify The user’s real intent The user’s reply in multi-turn interaction flash is 0/3 throughout, while Qwen is 3/3 throughout Going back to the logs and querying the detailed output, we can see that on the negative test cases, qwen and V3 both managed to ask clarifying questions, for example:
Qwen (case 55): 请提供具体信息: 您希望查询哪一天的数据？或者您是否有特定的指标名称（index_name）和指标类别（index_category）？
(Ask for specific information: which day’s data would you like to query, or do you have a particular metric name (index_name) and metric category (index_category)?)
V3 (case 60): 引导提问: 请问您想查询哪个具体的指标名称(index_name)？因为表中有多个指标类别(index_category)和指标名称(index_name)，需要明确要对比的具体指标。
(A guiding question: which specific metric name (index_name) would you like to query? The table has several metric categories (index_category) and metric names (index_name), so the specific metric to compare needs to be specified.)
By contrast, flash indiscriminately produced hypothetical SQL output for all 90 questions, for instance defaulting a missing range to the whole table (把缺失的范围默认成"整表") or a missing time to a concrete time slice (把缺失的时间默认成具体的时间切片). This is very close to flash’s failure mode in §3.2.2.
3.4 Cost # Cost metrics are split into two groups here: economic cost (how much each case costs) and experience cost (how long each case takes).
3.4.1 Economic Cost # Start with the detailed table, where:
input tokens = system prompt + schema injection + retrieved knowledge + user question; output tokens = the SQL or clarifying text the model actually generated this time; cached share = the share of input that hit the provider’s prompt cache (the cached part is billed at the lower cache price). Model · System calls / case input tokens / case output tokens / case total cached share CNY / 1k cases Qwen · direct 1.0 438 54 492 94.0% 0.46 Qwen · direct+rag 1.0 1,509 48 1,557 84.0% 1.19 Qwen · harness 1.0 1,509 48 1,557 96.0% 1.19 V3 · direct 1.0 425 52 476 0.0% 1.26 V3 · direct+rag 1.0 1,404 65 1,470 0.0% 3.33 V3 · harness 1.0 1,404 66 1,470 0.0% 3.34 flash · direct 1.0 427 52 479 60.0% 0.77 flash · direct+rag 1.0 1,406 62 1,469 74.0% 1.28 flash · harness 1.0 1,406 65 1,471 84.0% 1.02 For readability, costs below are reported uniformly in CNY per 1k cases.
The figure shows that, because each system runs only a single turn in this test, harness and direct+rag cost almost the same per 1k cases. The main reason is that the output contract layer is a purely software-side change and produces no tokens. Adding retrieval greatly increases the input, which is what drives cost up. Beyond that, the remaining cost differences come mainly from the provider. For example, V3 on SiliconFlow has a 0% cache hit rate, so all its input is billed at full price. And flash, because caching works, is actually cheaper than V3.
In summary, the most expensive of the three is the harness system on V3, at CNY 3.34 per 1k cases. At ten thousand calls a day, that is roughly CNY 33/day; switching to the Qwen model at the same volume costs about CNY 12/day.
3.4.2 Experience Cost # The figure shows directly that latency is set almost entirely by the model or provider, and is unrelated to input length. The clearest evidence is that after adding retrieval, none of the three models’ latency changed noticeably. What is worth noting is that flash’s latency is the smallest of the three, only a quarter of V3’s.
Putting the two together: adding retrieval “costs a little money and almost no experience”, while the model or model provider is the main source of economic-cost differences.
4. Conclusion # 4.1 Conclusion # Putting the three metric groups of §2.4 together, the conclusions are as follows.
On the quality dimension, retrieval is the only order-of-magnitude gain: with the same model and the same prompt, adding retrieval alone lifts EX from 6.9%/9.6%/32.9% to 43.8%/53.4%/54.8%. And the output contract layer in the architecture is only text processing on the final output; its gain shrinks as the system’s own executability rises, for instance the EX increment on direct+rag shrinks from Qwen’s +11.0 to V3’s +2.8, then to flash’s 0.0.
On the behavior dimension, retrieval is just as important. It lifts behavior decisions from the zero-ability line to 79.4% to 89.5% balanced accuracy, and fills in the refuse class of tasks to 12/14. But it must still be made clear that clarify and refuse are two abilities: the former is decided by the model throughout (Qwen 3/3, flash 0/3), while only the latter is a retrieval gain (§3.3.3).
On the cost dimension, retrieval can be called cheap and nearly free in experience. Input tokens rise to about 3.4×, but cost per 1k cases stays within CNY 3.34, and latency barely changes. The cost differences are mainly set by the provider’s unit price and caching policy, unrelated to the three systems under test.
In short, in single-turn conversation, the NL2SQL Agent architecture’s value is carried mainly by retrieval and the prompt. The part of its architecture that handles multi-turn interaction, information integration and output was not in scope this time, so extrapolation should be cautious (see §4.3).
The reason retrieval’s gain in single-turn generation is so pronounced is that it is essentially data processing, only over “text” rather than the tabular data (tabular data) that traditional data analysis is used to. Bringing these unstructured / semi-structured data, the database schema, metric definitions and business rules, through business analysis, text distillation and retrieval on demand, and finally feeding them to the model, this whole flow is itself another data pipeline. So the value of this NL2SQL Agent in single-turn conversation can be said to come almost entirely from text data engineering.
4.2 How Model Selection Affects the Results # In §2.3.2 I explained this selection, which was meant to cover three possible influencing factors: activation scale, domain bias and cost tier. After the experiment we can see that these three axes affect the results to different degrees.
Activation scale affects SQL quality, but the difference is only between Qwen and the other two. Splitting the 73 answerable cases by difficulty: Qwen flash V3 output-side activated params 3.3B 16B (output side) 37B medium EX 57% 67% 65% hard EX 12% 25% 25% Qwen lags systematically on both medium and hard (9~13pp, beyond §3.1.1’s jitter band), while V3 and flash show no measurable difference. So the real parameter step is: the 3.3B tier versus anything above ten-odd B; further up (16B → 37B) there is no extra gain. Also, Qwen is a code-specialized model yet is the worst on hard, which suggests the real bottleneck on hard cases may be schema understanding and assembling multiple clauses, not whether the model can write code.
The abstention-behavior differences are rooted in each model’s own training and decoding, not in architecture. All three models are MoE, using the same prompt and retrieval, yet their abstention decisions are completely different:
Decoding mode: this time flash’s thinking mode was turned off, so it guesses directly on ambiguity; on direct it outputs 90/90 SQL statements, sending its behavior straight back to the zero-ability line. This was verified separately in the project: with the same flash, simply turning thinking on drops direct+rag’s presumption rate from 41.2% to 17.6% and harness’s from 29.4% to 11.8%. Post-training: “whether to ask” is closer to a behavior preference shaped by post-training; DeepSeek’s official documentation also states that flash went through larger-scale reinforcement-learning post-training. Still, even with thinking on, flash’s refuse on direct is still 0/14, so the decoding mode is only one reason. Cost has nothing to do with model ability, only with the provider tier. When each case runs a single turn, the price differences come almost entirely from the provider’s unit price and caching policy, not from the systems under test.
One-line summary: model selection’s influence concentrates in two places. On SQL correctness, Qwen lags systematically behind V3/flash; on abstention policy, it is decided by the model’s own decoding and post-training. A system’s running cost, meanwhile, is tied to the provider tier.
summary: An NL2SQL Agent translates natural-language questions into SQL, and its core design is to ask a clarifying question first when information is missing, mimicking real human interaction, rather than forcing an answer. Over the past year, as the harness idea spread and models kept getting stronger, I began to wonder whether the NL2SQL Agent I built actually has an ask-first advantage. That question is what produced this evaluation. The conclusion, up front: retrieval is the only order-of-magnitude gain. And because retrieval is essentially data processing over text, the Agent’s value in single-turn conversation comes almost entirely from text data engineering.
title: Does Text Data Engineering Matter Most? A Single-Turn Capability Evaluation of an NL2SQL Agent

Written by Human TL;DR A self-built agent that pauses to ask clarifying questions before generating SQL — instead of guessing at ambiguous requests like most NL2SQL chatbots do. Built on a small classifier, a dedicated SQL coder, and a business-context database dictionary to handle real-world schema ambiguity.
Previous Next xifanz42/nl2sql_agent 轻量化自然语言数据库查询工具，支持多轮对话完善查询目标，精确输出SQL查询语句、执行查询、数据分析并返回自然语言结果。A lightweight system enbales multiple rounds of chat to transfer natural language into SQL query, execute query, perform data analysis and return analysis results. Python 16 2 1. Background Inspiration This project was inspired by my first start-up trial project, where we meant to build a multi-agent consulting system using Dify in late 2024. I explored the full functionality of Dify back then, and realized a core limitation:
It doesn’t support a true agentic loop.
Chatflow lets you design a rich sequence of nodes and branches, but that sequence has to be hand-drawn in advance. The model itself has no way to decide, at runtime, whether it has enough information to act or needs to pause and ask the user something first.
Therefore, the multi-agent system I built on top of it is actually a sequential chatflow, with each step being an LLM equipped with some external tools or MCPs, rather than an agentic system that can interact with users back and forth.
The problem is even more obvious when users’ inputs can only be answered by querying a relational database (PostgreSQL, etc.), since a chatbot with no way to pause and clarify has only one option: guess.
A typical failed case looks like this:
User: I want to know the average stopping time
Chatbot: The average stopping time of red cars in Thailand is …
Apparently, the user failed to give a definition for the average stopping time. Because the flow had no way to pause and ask what that meant, the chatbot filled the gap itself using its own assumptions. Though the result looks like a hallucination, it isn’t really one — the model didn’t invent this out of nowhere; it did the only thing the architecture let it do.
Assumption Here I have to introduce a vital assumption (or reality):
Consumers are ignorant and fail at asking correct questions Consumers are incapable of clarifying their core needs because they inherently have limited information. Therefore, they typically fail to input a clear and correct question (prompt) in the initial few rounds.
Causal Analysis Under the above assumption, it becomes clear that the first cause of our system’s failure is the well-known term in data science — garbage in, garbage out. Garbage here is no longer data, but text.
The second cause of failure is more systemic and critical. From late 2024 to early 2025, Dify was still under active development. A complex system built on top of it would inevitably inherit Dify’s flaws as systemic flaws of its own. Without a true agentic loop, our system was unable to clarify the true problem behind users’ incorrect inputs, further weakening its response reliability.
Summary All in all, the root cause stems from two aspects:
unclear inputs systemic failure As a result, this NL2SQL Agent project aims to fix the core module of our multi-agent system, making the database query task more reliable.
The project is aiming for anyone who wants to interact with a database without knowing its details.
2. Solution In early 2025, I thought the best solution was to self-develop a minimal agent architecture — one with conversational memory that could itself determine whether the user’s input was sufficient to generate SQL.
So the first thing I designed was that the agent would be powered by multiple large language models, each with a specific purpose. I pre-defined three kinds of tasks — or roles, I should say:
A small helper for two simple tasks: to classify the user’s question to determine if the user needs to clarify further A coder responsible only for generating SQL A reasoner for syntheic response Besides this, there’s also a context engineering piece. Apart from normal RAG (embedding, chunking, retrieving etc.), how to clarify database schemas is another key point.
In reality, a single database could contain multiple columns with similar column names but slightly different business meanings. This is another source of the LLM fabricating its own response. To address this problem, my design back then was to prepare a human-written database dictionary and feed it into the RAG pipeline by default. The dictionary should at least contain the following information:
data field name (column name) data type data unit example value (few-shot examples) a short business explanation Later, I found that the following information is optional but can improve performance by more clearly defining the data boundary:
data category (if it’s categorical) data range (if it’s numerical) By design, the agent now has a better ability to ask follow-up questions for query clarification, and is equipped with a better understanding of the database from a business perspective.
3. Architecture Here’s a more detailed system architecture:
The agent supports both a web interface and a CLI. Beyond its core workflow, it also supports general exploratory interaction.
4. Demo Walkthrough Finally, here’s a demo walkthrough.
In this video, I deliberately asked a vague question about error logs at first. Instead of calling the coder to generate SQL and query the database, the agent asked a follow-up: whether I was looking for general error logs or logs for a specific vehicle. I replied that I was looking for a specific vehicle. The agent then asked further questions to narrow down the scope.

Translated by AI Reviewed by Human In One Sentence As the sole technical lead, I independently delivered the full-stack architecture for a Web3 compliance sales intelligence SaaS from 0 to 1 (PostgreSQL + row-level security + Next.js) and validated it with real paying B2B customers—making this a practical retrospective on technical decisions and commercialization trade-offs. Product Demo All data shown has been anonymized.
Your browser does not support the video tag. Previous Next About the Project 1. Background Why did we build it? Between 2024 and 2025, major crypto regulatory frameworks gradually moved from the legislation stage into mandatory enforcement. As regulations became clearer, two new customer groups emerged: companies that needed compliance services (buyers), and companies that made money by selling compliance services (sellers).
However, the latter still relied on manual prospect lists and generic CRMs for customer acquisition. These traditional approaches could not answer questions created by the new regulatory environment, such as:
What licenses does this company hold? Is the license currently active, pending, or expired?
Who was it built for? Given these limitations, we focused on the sell side of the Web3 compliance ecosystem—BD and sales teams at custodians, on-chain auditing and KYT providers, compliance consultancies, cross-border payment companies, and blockchain security firms.
Their daily work is not simply about finding companies. It is about determining whether a company currently has a compliance need, who it is connected to, and where the risks are.
2. What We Built Compliance-Anchored Profiles Using Hong Kong SFC-licensed institutions as anchors, we centralized information such as license status and sanctions matches instead of leaving it scattered across raw source lists. Entity Relationship Graph Starting from a licensed entity, users could trace parent companies, subsidiaries, and investment relationships, with relationship weights inherited based on license relevance. Structured Intelligence Profiles A company’s basic information, licensing and compliance records, related entities, and relevant contacts were consolidated into a searchable profile. Staged Lead Delivery Users entered their target industries and customers, and trial leads were unlocked in three batches based on account age, with all leads unlocked within 15 days. Behavior Tracking & Feedback Searches, saves, dismissals, and recommendation ratings were stored to provide data for the next iteration of ranking and recommendation. 3. My Role Sole Technical Lead Full-Stack Technical Decisions & Architecture: Defined the overall technology stack, deployment approach, and frontend/backend boundaries based on the permission, compliance, and responsiveness requirements of a B2B data SaaS. Core Data & Permission Design: Designed the company relationship data model around Hong Kong SFC-licensed institutions and established quality standards for cleaning, validating, and ingesting data from multiple sources. Product UX & Admin Management: Designed the overall information architecture, routing, and page structure for the product; separated the marketing website from the product console; and built an admin backend for data and permission management. My team also included two data engineering interns. I broke down their tasks and defined detailed acceptance criteria, and they did an excellent job with data collection, preprocessing, and initial quality validation.
4. System Architecture 5. Results 12,388
License Data Records
A company data foundation aligned around Hong Kong SFC-licensed institutions 732
Real User Actions
Including 35 explicit ratings of recommendation results 31
Companies Delivered to Real Customers
Across one paying B2B customer and one B2B trial customer 53 / 30 / 24 / 50+
Migrations / Tables / RPCs / RLS Policies
Complete database-side delivery, with row-level security enabled on 30 tables The Story Behind It As the sole technical lead, I was responsible for both the frontend and backend. The most mentally demanding part was no longer writing code—it was deciding what to prioritize when resources were limited and information was incomplete.
At the beginning, I had a lot of questions: Should I build the backend from scratch or use an existing BaaS? As someone who had barely touched frontend development (unless Streamlit counts), how could I deliver something customer-facing within a realistic timeframe? What does a typical SaaS architecture actually look like?
So in this section, I want to discuss two backend and database-related decisions I made during this project.
1. Technical Decisions 1.1 Using UUIDv5 for Cross-Source Entity Resolution Back when I was building toy projects at university, I would often receive a dataset and immediately add an auto-incrementing primary key. But that approach obviously does not work in a real product.
For our data assets in particular, building multidimensional intelligence about a company required combining information from multiple sources. The same entity could appear in different batches, different data sources, and under different source IDs in the main table.
So how could we ensure that newly ingested data would still correctly match entities already in the database instead of creating duplicates?
My first idea was to use UUIDv5 to create deterministic primary keys. As long as the logic used to generate the ID was unique, this could avoid the problem above.
But that immediately raised another question: Which attributes should be used to construct the ID so that it is both uniquely deterministic and useful for aligning entities across sources?
My approach was to define a priority order for each data source:
Use the most deterministic and unique identifier available in that source as the first choice for constructing the logical primary key.
For example, the CE Reference number in the SFC licensed entity list is issued by the regulator and globally unique, so it could be used as the unique identifier in the ID generation logic.
If a source did not contain a unique identifier—for example, an SFC alert list containing only a company name—we would fall back to a cleaned combination of company name + country code. Of course, when company names are used as a fallback, they need to be standardized consistently. For example, "Tencent Co. Ltd." and "tencent" must first be normalized into the same string before they can generate the same ID.
Once the IDs for company entities in the main table are deterministic, generating IDs for child tables becomes much simpler. I will not go into that in detail here.
There is one important caveat, though: while deterministic IDs solve the problem of uniqueness, they do not automatically solve cross-source entity matching.
For cross-source matching, we used a separate approach in the data cleaner: exact matching combined with substring-based fuzzy matching.
1.2 Moving Trial Lead Distribution Logic into the Database During onboarding, our product asked new users to enter their target customers or companies they had already worked with. Based on that information, the system selected 15 companies from the database and recommended them as trial sales leads.
These leads were not released all at once. Instead, they were progressively unlocked in three batches over the lifecycle of the account.
At the time, I spent quite a while deciding which layer this lead distribution logic should live in.
From a conventional engineering perspective, the obvious choice would be the application layer: write the company selection logic in Node.js and add a cron job to unlock additional leads at the appropriate time.
But given our actual situation, that approach had one major downside: higher development cost.
For a team with only one technical developer, adding another middle layer did not simply mean adding another layer. It also meant service integration, business workflow orchestration, deployment testing, and more—at least another week on the schedule.
That was difficult to justify when we were under significant time pressure and had limited resources. Our priority was not only to launch quickly, but also to ensure that data was distributed accurately to different users without cross-user contamination.
So I temporarily decided to:
Put this business logic directly in the database layer and keep lead distribution logic as close to the data itself as possible.
The entire workflow was ultimately implemented as two PostgreSQL functions:
generate_trial_leads was responsible for selecting companies and assigning batches. It first filtered company data based on the information users provided during onboarding, then ranked the remaining companies by priority and assigned them "batch1", "batch2", or "batch3" labels. get_trial_leads was responsible for deciding which leads a user should see right now. Instead of storing which batch had been unlocked, it calculated the account’s age dynamically by subtracting the account creation time from the current time, then determined which batches should be available based on the number of active days. 2. How the Project Ended After eight months of exploration, the project was shut down in April 2026.
After discussing it with my co-founder, we realized that the business direction still had several fundamental problems.
We had answered the question of “who is safer?”, but what customers actually wanted to know was “who can become a customer?”
We delivered “who exists”. They wanted sales leads they could directly act on.
We provided structured entity and compliance intelligence, while customers expected leads that could help move sales forward immediately.
This was not a technical failure. It was a product-market and demand mismatch.
3. Looking Back from Today This has been the startup project into which I have invested the most effort, spent the longest amount of time, and had the greatest degree of autonomy. It also ultimately acquired real paying B2B customers. That is why it remains an experience I revisit repeatedly: What did I learn? What did I do right? What could I have done better?
I see the lessons from both a business and a technical perspective.
First thing first, the clearest business lesson was:
Validate demand broadly before you start writing code.
At the beginning of this project, I consistently saw myself primarily as the technical person. But as a co-founder, I overlooked something more important: validating whether the market actually wanted the product, and distinguishing genuine purchase signals from polite encouragement.
For developers facing a similar problem, I highly recommend The Mom Test. It provides a very practical explanation of what genuine buying signals look like and how to design questions that actually test market demand.
If I had read it earlier, perhaps instead of spending so much time researching data sources, building the backend, and designing the frontend, I would have started with something much lighter—perhaps just a single landing page.
Now, on to the technical side.
I also fell into a common trap for startup developers: endlessly expanding within the areas I already understood, diving deeper into details, and trying to make the first version robust enough from the beginning. I invested a great deal of time in database design and data management. To be fair, LeadX was itself a data product, so the data foundation was part of the product itself. The real problem was that I failed to distinguish between two kinds of variables:
Things that should be standardized and established early because they are foundational. Things that will change rapidly as the product evolves and therefore need to remain flexible. From a purely architectural perspective, our product followed a thick frontend, no middle layer, database-heavy (BaaS) architecture. This is a mainstream product architecture that has already been validated by many indie SaaS products, and if I were building the product again, I would still choose this overall architecture.
However, I would not take the same shortcut when it came to business logic orchestration. I thought I was saving time by avoiding a middle layer. But by doing so, I accidentally placed the most frequently changing business logic inside the container with the highest cost of modification: the database.
So if I were doing it again, I would let the depth at which logic is pushed down follow the pace of validation:
I would still build foundational infrastructure early and build it properly. But before receiving real payment signals, rapidly changing business logic and fancy algorithmic work should remain as shallow and flexible as possible.
Returning to the context of this startup: technology’s most important role is to serve business goals as a tool and means of execution.
Only after the business survives does it make sense to optimize, iterate, and add more high-tech capabilities.
summary: As the sole technical lead, I built a Web3 compliance sales intelligence SaaS from 0 to 1—independently delivering the frontend, backend, database, and row-level security architecture, validating the product with real paying B2B customers, and developing practical lessons around technical decision-making and demand validation.
title: LeadX: Building a Full-Stack Web3 Compliance Sales Intelligence SaaS from 0 to 1
